slides.title: Architecture. Theater. Emerging technology.
slides.note: Here are the things I love. This is the story of how they became interesting to me, and how they became a job. I hope it sparks an idea about the things you love.

slides.title: “Pick a lane”
slides.note: Richard Rosa told me to pick a lane. I think people who tell you to focus on one thing are telling you what worked for their brain. They are trying to help. My brain was excited to jump between things.
My interests kept pulling in different directions. Architecture, theater, emerging technology.
I was looking for places where those interests could work together. Establish cyan architecture, rose theater and violet technology, matching the tracker.

slides.title: One deliberate line
slides.note: At Syracuse we were not allowed to touch a computer for the first year. At the time it was excruciating. It made me think deliberately about every line and every line weight. With Revit you make a wall, and the lines are a byproduct. Clarity can get lost.

slides.note: In third-year comprehensive studio Brian Lonsway was teaching MicroStation. He let me teach myself Revit instead. That led to internships at VIP Structures and Redleaf Corporation. slides.title: Fisher Dachs Associates
slides.note: I got to be an architect specializing in theaters. Two of my interests in one job. And still I felt a gap: where was the emerging technology? It felt like complaining about the sheen of the gold on the wall. A very first-world problem.

slides.title: Oculus Rift DK1
slides.note: A year later the DK1 arrived. Josh Dachs, my boss and later co-founder, let me focus on it. I thought I would just drop the 3ds Max, Rhino and SketchUp models in.

slides.title: It wasn’t turnkey
slides.note: In 2013 there was no elegant turnkey way to do what I expected. I went home at night and learned JavaScript and C# on Codecademy, learned Unity, learned model optimization. Architecture school taught me modeling, not optimization. It was exactly the kind of challenge I loved going home to.

slides.title: Josh’s office
slides.note: Early 2016: Josh pulled me in and said he felt I was thinking of leaving to start a VR company. My reaction was, What? No! I will work here till I die. Then he said I was not much of a business manager, not organized, with creative wildfire but not much direction. I thought he was trying to convince me not to leave. These are paraphrased delivery prompts from the walk, not a verbatim historical transcript.

slides.title: “We should do it together”
slides.note: Then Josh said that if I really wanted to start a VR company, we should do it together. That was the surprise. We founded Agile Lens later in 2016. Ten years now. Show people how passionate you are, including what you do off-hours because you love it. That is how they come to believe in you.

slides.title: Curiosity
slides.note: When I hire, I am not looking first at GPA or whether someone studied VR. Excitement, being a quick study, curiosity. Be curious, not judgmental, as Ted Lasso puts it. I knew talented architects whose presentations looked like watching paint dry. I would have been thrilled to show work like theirs.

slides.title: VR is like the early days of film
slides.note: One camera films an action. Then cuts connect angles and time: the next day. Montage makes relationships. A close-up feels different from a wide. Tilting the camera can make us uneasy. That language developed over time. VR is still young. Dated milestones, not first-invention claims: Lumière 1895 (ACMI); Porter 1903 (MoMA/LOC); Pig Alley 1912 (MoMA); Intolerance 1916 (BFI); expressionist geometry 1920s (Deutsche Kinemathek); Eisenstein 1925 (MoMA). Dutch tilt first use NEEDS CONFIRMATION, do not claim a first.
